This is a plan, not a special mode; I haven’t started implementation. Reply `go` to execute this plan, or tell me what to change.

## Goal

Turn Stranded Horizons from the current single-player vanilla-JS wave shooter into **Stranded Horizons v2: Persistent One World F2P** as described in the README — one persistent world, one permanently assigned chunk/base per player, distance-based factory efficiency, server-authoritative factory building, factions, an admin world panel, Minecraft world import, and scalable hosting on the owner's KVM/VPS — without losing the existing playable v1 game during the transition.

Researched in this single session only (no sub-agents used). No code was changed.

## Current state (verified from the repo)

| Fact | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Stack today | Pure vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no build step, no backend, no dependencies, no `package.json` |
| Entry points | [index.html](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/index.html) landing with Play Now → [game.html](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/game.html) |
| All game logic | One monolithic [game.js](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/game.js), 1,355 lines, one class, `requestAnimationFrame` loop, WASD/mouse/touch, waves, shop, meta-progression |
| Persistence today | Only `localStorage` (meta progression, best run), already hardened with strict validation — see [SECURITY_REVIEW.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/SECURITY_REVIEW.md) finding 1, fixed in commit `05a7156` |
| Deploy today | Vercel static hosting with cache headers in [vercel.json](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/vercel.json); assets immutable-cached 1 year |
| Repo hygiene rules | [rules.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/rules.md): vanilla, readable small functions, centralised tuning values, preserve existing gameplay unless intentionally changed, docs kept in sync |
| Known open compliance item | [SECURITY_REVIEW.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/SECURITY_REVIEW.md) finding 2: no per-asset licence/provenance manifest for `assets/` (~37 images) — must be fixed before any F2P/commercial v2 launch |
| Recent history | Security hardening, mobile/touch controls, wave-spawn fix, Vercel caching — v1 is actively maintained, so v2 must be additive, not a rewrite that breaks v1 |

## Problems and contradictions in the README v2 sketch (resolve before coding)

These were found by re-reading the README closely. Implementing agents must not silently pick a side; each needs the decision recorded in `docs/v2/DECISIONS.md` (Step 0.4).

1. **Efficiency numbers don't match.** Text says centre = 100%, edge at distance 7,000 = 30%. The formula `max(30, 100 - distanz/200)` gives 65% at 7,000 and only hits the 30% floor at 14,000. The JS snippet `Math.max(30, 100 - d * 0.005)` is identical to `/200`, so the *text* is wrong, not the code. Decision needed: keep formula (floor at 14,000) or steepen to reach 30% at 7,000 (`100 - d/100`).
2. **World/chunk geometry is ambiguous.** "20000x20000 virtuelle Einheiten, aufgeteilt in 100x100 Chunks" can mean 100×100 = 10,000 chunks of 200×200 units, or chunks of 100×100 units = 40,000 chunks. This changes DB size, worker sharding (Phase 5 uses 1000x1000 areas), and the scatter algorithm. Must be fixed in one ADR before schema work.
3. **Scatter placement is unspecified.** "kein Grid, random verteilt, Wege dazwischen" — no algorithm, no minimum distance, no collision/retry rule, no determinism/seed. Needs a spec (e.g. Poisson-disc / jittered grid with min-distance and max-attempts + fallback) or chunk assignment will deadlock as the world fills.
4. **No identity/auth in the sketch.** "Beim ersten Login" assumes accounts, but no auth system, session, or anti-multi-account rule is defined. This blocks Phase 0 schema (`owner` in `bases`) and all of monetisation. Biggest missing decision in the plan.
5. **No economy model.** Buildings "produziert", server "prüft Ressourcen" — but resources, production rates, costs, offline production, and caps are undefined. Phase 2 cannot be built or balanced without a resource/building table first.
6. **Redis appears in Phase 3 before it's introduced.** Admin writes MariaDB + `redis.publish('chunk:update', …)`, but Redis is only justified later by multi-worker scaling. Decide: introduce Redis in Phase 0 (needed anyway for the Socket.IO adapter once >1 server process runs) or defer to Phase 5.
7. **Monetisation has no payment, legal, or ToS workstream.** Selling base slots/boosters (even cosmetics) needs a payment provider, refund/consumer law handling (DE/EU), and a decision on the booster-vs-"ohne Pay2Win" tension the README itself creates (paid efficiency booster at the edge is arguably pay-to-win). Flagged as a product decision, not an engineering task.
8. **Minecraft import licensing.** Importing "1000 SpigotMC Maps" raises map-author licence/redistribution rights. Needs a rights check per imported map before public placement, same class of risk as SECURITY_REVIEW finding 2.

## Key decisions (recommended, with alternatives rejected)

| # | Decision | Recommendation | Why / rejected alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Repo layout | Keep one repo; add `server/`, `db/`, `shared/`, `admin/`, `tools/mc-import/`. Client stays at repo root on Vercel | Matches README Phase 0 and existing Vercel deploy; a monorepo split would break auto-deploy and history for zero benefit at this scale |
| D2 | Server stack | Node.js + Express + Socket.IO v4 on the KVM, exactly as README says | Socket.IO gives rooms/namespaces, automatic transport fallback (long-polling → WebSocket/WebTransport) and a Redis adapter for multi-process broadcast — confirmed in official docs. Rejected: raw `ws` (reinvents rooms/reconnect/acks), Colyseus (extra framework, team has no experience evidenced in repo) |
| D3 | Source of truth | Server-authoritative simulation tick (README: every 2s) in MariaDB; client only sends intents (`place`, `connect`, …) and renders state | README explicitly wants this to kill cheating. Rejected: client-authoritative with server validation (keeps cheat surface, contradicts README) |
| D4 | Database | MariaDB with JSON column for `blueprint_json`, per README's `bases` table | Owner already plans MariaDB; MariaDB supports JSON, spatial and standard types per official reference. Rejected: PostgreSQL (better JSON/spatial, but contradicts owner's infra plan and adds a new system to operate) |
| D5 | Realtime fan-out | Redis pub/sub from Phase 0, used for (a) Socket.IO adapter, (b) `chunk:update` admin events | Redis pub/sub is at-most-once — acceptable for "reload this chunk" hints, **not** for economy/production state, which must always be re-read from MariaDB. Redis must never be exposed publicly: the Socket.IO Redis adapter docs warn its channels are unauthenticated and anyone who can publish can forge client events |
| D6 | Tick model | One simulation worker process per world shard; idempotent tick keyed by `(chunk_id, tick_number)` so a restarted worker never double-produces | Prevents the classic offline-production double-count bug; enables Phase 5 sharding later without redesign |
| D7 | Admin panel | Separate `admin/` app (own auth, own deploy), reusing the owner's existing management-panel pattern (`:5173/:3001`) as README suggests; Leaflet with `CRS.Simple` for the world map | Leaflet's API supports non-geographic maps via custom CRS/latlng conversion. Rejected: building admin into the game client (privilege-escalation surface), Google/Mapbox tiles (cost, wrong abstraction for a game world) |
| D8 | MC import | Offline Python service using Amulet-Core to read world data (Amulet manipulates Minecraft world data in Python; PyMCTranslate handles block translation between versions), mapping via versioned `mc_to_sh.json`, outputting blueprint JSON only — never writing the live DB directly | Keeps the risky parser off the game server; every import goes through admin preview → explicit place. Rejected: parsing `.schematic`/region files in Node (immature ecosystem), auto-placing imports without preview |
| D9 | v1 game | Freeze v1 gameplay; keep it reachable as "Arcade/Wave mode" while v2 is built behind a separate route | [rules.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/rules.md) requires preserving existing behaviour; gives an instant fallback if v2 slips |
| D10 | Auth (open, see Risks) | Default assumption until owner decides: lightweight account (name + password, hashed, server-side sessions over the Socket.IO handshake), no email required for v2-alpha | Needed to make `bases.owner` real. OAuth-only and wallet/crypto identity are rejected as scope creep |

## Approach

Build v2 as five gated phases exactly following the README's order (foundation → efficiency/placement → factories → admin → MC import → scaling/monetisation), but insert a **Phase 0.0 decision/spec gate** first, because contradictions 1–5 above make Phases 1–2 unbuildable as written. Each phase ships behind a feature flag / separate route so v1 on Vercel never breaks. Every phase ends with a playable or operable increment, automated tests, and a docs update, per [rules.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/rules.md) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/CONTRIBUTING.md).

Suggested agent workstreams (for the owner's future multi-agent loop, one owner per stream, no two agents editing the same file concurrently):

- **Agent A — Server/Simulation:** `server/`, tick loop, chunk assignment, efficiency, factory rules.
- **Agent B — Client:** v2 Canvas client, world/chunk rendering, build UI, socket client; v1 files read-only.
- **Agent C — Data/Infra:** `db/` migrations, Docker Compose (MariaDB, Redis, server), KVM deploy, NGINX/WebSocket proxying, monitoring.
- **Agent D — Admin:** `admin/` panel, Leaflet live map, chunk editor, world events, in-game `:` console.
- **Agent E — MC Import:** `tools/mc-import/` Python service, `mc_to_sh.json`, preview generation.
- **Agent F — QA/Docs (rotating):** tests, `ASSETS_LICENSES.md`, README/rules sync, playtest checklists. Every phase PR requires F's checklist before merge.

## Steps

### Phase 0.0 — Decisions & specs (gate, ~2–3 days, no production code)

0.1. Write `docs/v2/DECISIONS.md` resolving contradictions 1–6: efficiency curve (pick exact formula + worked table at d = 0/1k/3k/7k/10k/14k), world geometry (world size, chunk size, chunk count), scatter algorithm (min distance, attempts, seed, behaviour when full), auth model (D10 or owner's alternative), resource list v1 (suggest: iron, energy, components), building list v1 (Mine, Förderband, Fabrik, Mauer, Turm per README) with cost/rate table.
0.2. Write `docs/v2/PROTOCOL.md`: every Socket.IO event, direction, payload schema, error codes, ack/timeout behaviour, version field. Client intents only; server never trusts client-computed resources, positions outside the player's chunk, or efficiency values.
0.3. Write `docs/v2/SCHEMA.md`: full MariaDB schema (below) with indexes, uniqueness constraints, and migration policy.
0.4. Owner sign-off on 0.1–0.3. **No Phase 0 code before this gate passes.**

Proposed schema (to be confirmed in 0.3): `users(id, name UNIQUE, pass_hash, created_at)`, `bases(id, owner_id FK, chunk_x, chunk_y, world_x, world_y, efficiency_cached, blueprint_json JSON, created_at, UNIQUE(world_x, world_y), UNIQUE(owner_id, slot))`, `faction_links(base_a, base_b, status, created_at, PRIMARY KEY(base_a, base_b))` with both-confirm workflow, `buildings(chunk_id, grid_x, grid_y, type, level, state_json, PRIMARY KEY(chunk_id, grid_x, grid_y))`, `resources(chunk_id, resource, amount, updated_at_tick)`, `ticks(id, shard, tick_number, applied_at, UNIQUE(shard, tick_number))`, `admin_audit(id, admin, action, payload_json, created_at)`, `imports(id, source_file, mapping_version, blueprint_json, placed_chunk, created_by)`.

### Phase 0 — Foundation (README: 1–2 weeks)

0.5. `server/` scaffold: Express + Socket.IO, config from env (no secrets in repo, per CONTRIBUTING), `/health` endpoint, structured logging, graceful shutdown. Node ≥ 18 per Express install docs.
0.6. `db/` migrations (versioned SQL, up-only in prod) creating the 0.3 schema; seed script for a dev world.
0.7. Docker Compose for local dev + KVM: `mariadb`, `redis` (internal network only, never published), `server`. NGINX reverse proxy terminating TLS and proxying WebSocket upgrade to the Node process; Vercel frontend connects cross-origin to `wss://<ws-host>` with an explicit CORS allowlist (production domain + localhost only).
0.8. Auth slice: register/login/logout, hashed passwords, session token checked in the Socket.IO handshake middleware; reject unauthenticated sockets. Rate-limit auth and all mutating events.
0.9. Chunk assignment service: on first authenticated login, run the 0.1 scatter algorithm inside a DB transaction, insert the `bases` row, return the assignment; repeat logins return the same chunk forever (idempotency test required). Store `efficiency_cached` computed server-side by the decided formula.
0.10. Client vertical slice: new route/page (v1 untouched) that logs in, connects, receives its chunk, and renders own chunk + efficiency % + chunk colour fading with worsening efficiency (README Phase 1 UI requirement pulled forward as the Phase 0 proof).
0.11. CI: lint + server unit tests + a boot smoke test (compose up → health → socket connect → chunk assigned) on every PR.

### Phase 1 — Efficiency & faction links (README Phase 1)

1.1. `server/world.js`: single `getEfficiency(x, y)` implementing the 0.1-decided formula; unit tests pinning the worked table from 0.1 so formula and docs can never drift again.
1.2. Faction link flow: `link:request` → other owner gets pending request → `link:confirm`/`link:reject`; on confirm, both bases gain +10% efficiency, hard-capped at 100%, recomputed server-side; unlink removes the bonus. Store link state only in `faction_links`; never cache the bonus without recompute on read-after-write.
1.3. Client: show base efficiency, link state, pending requests; chunk colour scale documented in UI legend.
1.4. Abuse cases: self-link, duplicate link, linking a non-existent/offline owner, link spam (rate limit + one pending request per pair).

### Phase 2 — Factories (README Phase 2, Factorio-light)

2.1. Build grid: each chunk exposes a 20×20 grid; `place`/`remove`/`upgrade` socket intents validated server-side for ownership, grid bounds, occupancy, and resource cost. Every rejection returns a typed error from PROTOCOL.md.
2.2. Simulation tick (2s): production/consumption for Mine → Förderband → Fabrik chains, turret/wall as static state in v1 of this phase; all arithmetic server-side, persisted per tick with the D6 idempotency key; offline production computed from elapsed ticks on load, capped per 0.1 economy table.
2.3. Client build UI: palette, ghost preview, costs, production rates, chunk inventory; render only server-sent state (no client-side resource math beyond display formatting).
2.4. Anti-cheat pass: fuzz every mutating event with out-of-range coordinates, negative amounts, foreign chunk IDs, and replayed messages; server must reject all without state change.

### Phase 3 — Admin (README Phase 3)

3.1. `admin/` app with separate admin auth (allowlisted accounts + audit log on every write). Routes: `/admin/world` live Leaflet map (`CRS.Simple`, chunk rectangles coloured by efficiency, click → chunk detail), chunk JSON editor with schema validation before save, manual efficiency override (stored as override, visibly marked, audited), structure placement using the same server validation path as players.
3.2. World events: admin action that places N ruin/bunker structures into eligible old chunks; implemented as a normal server-side placement batch + Redis `chunk:update` publish so online workers reload affected chunks (MariaDB remains the truth; Redis is only a reload hint, at-most-once is acceptable because clients also re-fetch on reconnect).
3.3. In-game `:` console for admins only (server re-checks admin flag on every command): `:tp x y`, `:give <resource> <amount>`, `:place <type>`; every console action writes to `admin_audit`. Non-admin attempts are rejected and logged.
3.4. Safety: admin writes require confirmation for destructive actions, all admin endpoints behind the private network/VPN or IP allowlist in addition to auth, and a tested DB backup/restore runbook before admin goes live.

### Phase 4 — Minecraft import (README Phase 4)

4.1. `tools/mc-import/` Python service (owner's Python focus): upload of `.schematic`/`.schem`/`region/` via the admin panel only, stored quarantined, size/type limits, malware-safe handling (no execution of uploaded content).
4.2. Parser spike first: prove Amulet-Core can read one real Java world/region and one schematic from the owner's collection and enumerate blocks; if a format is unsupported, record it and descope that format rather than writing a hand parser.
4.3. `mc_to_sh.json` mapping (versioned, in-repo): start from the README's four mappings (stone→metal_wall, iron_block→factory_t1, chest→loot_container, spawner→enemy_spawner); unmapped blocks → explicit `ignore` or `unknown` bucket counted in the import report, never silently dropped.
4.4. Transform → blueprint JSON conforming to the Phase 2 building schema, with a 2D/3D preview in the admin panel; placement is a separate explicit admin action into a chosen chunk (as dungeon/ruin), reusing Phase 3 placement + audit. Imports never overwrite a player's base without an explicit override confirmation.
4.5. Rights gate: each imported map records source + licence/permission in `imports` and an `IMPORTS_LICENSES.md`; unlicensed maps stay in a private test world only.

### Phase 5 — Hosting, scale, monetisation (README Phase 5)

5.1. Sharding: partition the world into 1000×1000 areas, one worker container each, Socket.IO Redis adapter for cross-worker broadcast; infra automation starts a worker when its area exceeds 80% occupancy (metric defined in 0.3: assigned chunks / capacity). Load test must prove the 80% trigger before it is trusted.
5.2. Hardening & ops: backups (automated, restore-tested), monitoring/alerting on the owner's existing tooling, error tracking, tick-lag and socket-connection dashboards, incident runbook.
5.3. Monetisation (only after legal/product decisions in Risks): free base, paid 2nd base slot (one-time), cosmetics, edge efficiency booster (7 days, never above 100%) — implemented as entitlements on `users`, granted only by verified payment webhooks; no payment code before provider + EU consumer-law review.
5.4. Public launch gate: `ASSETS_LICENSES.md` complete (SECURITY_REVIEW finding 2), privacy policy/ToS live, data-export/delete for accounts, load test + 7-day closed beta with rollback plan (v1 remains live throughout).

### Cross-cutting (every phase)

- Docs updated in the same PR as behaviour ([rules.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/rules.md), [CONTRIBUTING.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/CONTRIBUTING.md)): README, PROTOCOL.md, SCHEMA.md, DECISIONS.md.
- No secrets, logs, build artefacts, or uploaded world files committed.
- Conventional commit messages per repo history (`feat:`, `docs:`, `fix:` style already in use); one PR per numbered step where practical; no agent merges its own PR without the QA checklist.

## Success criteria

- v1 game at [game.html](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/game.html) still plays exactly as today after every phase.
- A new player can register, log in, and permanently receives the same chunk on every later login; efficiency shown matches the documented formula at known coordinates.
- Two players can link bases by mutual confirmation and both receive +10% (capped 100%); unlinking removes it.
- A player can place/remove the five building types on their 20×20 grid; production accrues server-side every 2s and survives server restart and offline time without double-counting.
- No client-sent value (resources, efficiency, foreign chunk, out-of-grid placement) is ever accepted by the server in fuzz tests.
- An admin can view the live world map, edit/place with full audit trail, trigger a world event, and use the `:` console; a non-admin cannot.
- An admin can import a real Minecraft map file, preview the converted blueprint, and place it as a ruin/dungeon; unmapped blocks are reported, not lost.
- The system runs on the KVM behind NGINX with MariaDB + Redis private, monitored, backed up, and restore-tested.

## Validation plan

| Phase | Check | Expected evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 0.0 | Doc review of DECISIONS/PROTOCOL/SCHEMA against README | Every contradiction 1–6 has a recorded decision with numbers |
| 0 | Compose boot + socket smoke test in CI; manual login → chunk → relogin | Same chunk returned; health endpoint green; unauthenticated socket rejected |
| 0/1 | Unit tests for `getEfficiency` and scatter assignment | Pinned values at the 0.1 table coordinates; no duplicate/overlapping chunks in 1,000 simulated signups |
| 1 | Two-account manual + automated link flow test | Bonus applied only after both confirm; cap at 100%; unlink reverts |
| 2 | Tick idempotency test (run same tick twice, restart mid-tick); placement fuzz suite | Resources unchanged by duplicate tick; 100% of invalid placements rejected with typed errors |
| 2 | Soak test: 100 simulated chunks × 1h of ticks | No tick drift, no negative resources, bounded DB growth |
| 3 | Admin audit review; non-admin access attempts | Every write in `admin_audit`; all non-admin calls 403 + logged |
| 4 | Golden-file test: known map → expected blueprint JSON; import report | Block counts match, unknown blocks reported; preview equals placed result |
| 5 | Load test to the 80% shard trigger; backup restore drill | New worker starts and serves its area; restored DB passes smoke test |
| All | Browser playtest (desktop + mobile) of v1 and v2 routes | v1 unchanged; v2 slice usable on both |

Highest-risk validation: the Phase 2 tick-idempotency and anti-cheat fuzz suite — if production can double-count or be forged, the entire F2P economy is worthless, and every later phase inherits the flaw.

## Risks / open questions

- **Auth & account recovery (owner decision needed):** D10 assumes simple accounts. Email/OAuth, password reset, and multi-account abuse policy are undecided and block Phase 0.8 scope.
- **Economy numbers (owner decision needed):** resource/building costs and rates in 0.1 are placeholders until the owner playtests; Phase 2 balancing will need at least two tuning iterations.
- **Paid booster vs "kein Pay2Win":** the README promises no pay-to-win but sells an efficiency booster. Product/legal must resolve this before Phase 5.3; engineering should build entitlements generically so the booster can be dropped without rework.
- **Licensing:** game assets (SECURITY_REVIEW finding 2) and imported Minecraft maps both need provenance records before any public/commercial v2 launch.
- **KVM capacity unknown:** current VPS size, RAM, and bandwidth were not in the repo. Phase 5 sharding thresholds must be re-derived from a Phase 0 load test on the real box.
- **Redis exposure:** Redis and MariaDB must never be reachable from the internet; the Socket.IO Redis-adapter trust warning makes a misconfigured Redis a full event-forgery hole. Network check is part of the Phase 0 done-definition.
- **Scope risk:** Phases 3–5 each rival v1 in size. If time shrinks, cut in this order: monetisation → MC import formats beyond the proven spike → sharding automation (manual worker start is acceptable for a small beta). Never cut server-authoritative validation or backups.

# Plan

Read text file `SECURITY_REVIEW.md`.
1|# Security Review (2026-05-04)
2|
3|## Findings
4|
5|### 1) Unvalidated persistent deserialization from `localStorage` allows persistent state corruption / DoS-by-data
6|- **Where:** `game.js` `loadMetaProgress()` and `loadBestRun()` parse attacker-controlled `localStorage` and trust fields with no type/range checks.
7|- **Impact:** Any script running on the same origin (including browser extensions, compromised third-party scripts on the same host, or a user self-modifying state) can persist malformed values (e.g., strings, negative numbers, extreme values, objects) that break game invariants, produce `NaN` math propagation, or soft-lock logic across sessions.
8|- **Why this is a security issue:** This is insecure deserialization of untrusted persistent data in the browser context. While it does not enable RCE here, it enables persistent integrity loss and denial-of-service behavior.
9|- **Fix:** Validate parsed objects with a strict schema (numeric fields only, bounded ranges, defaults on invalid), and reject unknown keys before merging.
10|
11|### 2) GPL-3.0 distribution compliance risk: third-party asset provenance not documented
12|- **Where:** `assets/` contains numerous image files, but repository documentation does not provide per-asset license/provenance metadata.
13|- **Impact:** If any asset is sourced under non-GPL-compatible terms (or without redistribution rights), open-source distribution can violate copyright terms despite GPL-3.0 code licensing.
14|- **Why this is a security/compliance issue:** Licensing non-compliance is a legal supply-chain risk that can force takedowns or re-licensing.
15|- **Fix:** Add an `ASSETS_LICENSES.md` (or SPDX manifest) listing each asset, source URL/author, exact license, and compatibility status.
16|
17|## Scope checks completed
18|- Command injection: no shell/process execution paths found.
19|- Path traversal: no filesystem path handling APIs used.
20|- Hardcoded secrets: none found.
21|- Unsafe dependencies: no package manager / external runtime dependencies present in-repo.
22|- Race conditions & info-leaking error handling: no server-side concurrency surfaces; no sensitive exception disclosure observed.

# Introduction

tip

If you are new to Socket.IO, we recommend checking out our [tutorial](/docs/v4/tutorial/introduction).

## What Socket.IO is[​](#what-socketio-is "Direct link to What Socket.IO is")

Socket.IO is a library that enables **low-latency**, **bidirectional** and **event-based** communication between a client and a server.

![Diagram of a communication between a server and a client](/images/bidirectional-communication2.png)![Diagram of a communication between a server and a client](/images/bidirectional-communication2-dark.png)

The Socket.IO connection can be established with different low-level transports:

*   HTTP long-polling
*   [WebSocket](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API)
*   [WebTransport](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebTransport_API)

Socket.IO will automatically pick the best available option, depending on:

*   the capabilities of the browser (see [here](https://caniuse.com/websockets) and [here](https://caniuse.com/webtransport))
*   the network (some networks block WebSocket and/or WebTransport connections)

You can find more details about that in the ["How it works" section](/docs/v4/how-it-works/).



[`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe), [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe) and [`PUBLISH`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/publish) implement the [Publish/Subscribe messaging paradigm](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish/subscribe) where (citing Wikipedia) senders (publishers) are not programmed to send their messages to specific receivers (subscribers).
Rather, published messages are categorized into channels, without knowledge of what (if any) subscribers there may be.
Subscribers express interest in one or more channels and only receive messages that are of interest, without knowledge of what (if any) publishers there are.
This decoupling of publishers and subscribers allows for greater scalability and a more dynamic network topology.

For instance, to subscribe to channels "channel11" and "ch:00" the client issues a [`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe) providing the names of the channels:

```bash
SUBSCRIBE channel11 ch:00
```

Messages sent by other clients to these channels will be pushed by Redis to all the subscribed clients.
Subscribers receive the messages in the order that the messages are published.

A client subscribed to one or more channels shouldn't issue commands, although it can [`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe) and [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe) to and from other channels.
The replies to subscription and unsubscribing operations are sent in the form of messages so that the client can just read a coherent stream of messages where the first element indicates the type of message.
The commands that are allowed in the context of a subscribed RESP2 client are:

* [`PING`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/ping)
* [`PSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/psubscribe)
* [`PUNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/punsubscribe)
* [`QUIT`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/quit)
* [`RESET`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/reset)
* [`SSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/ssubscribe)
* [`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe)
* [`SUNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/sunsubscribe)
* [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe)

However, if RESP3 is used (see [`HELLO`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/hello)), a client can issue any commands while in the subscribed state.

Please note that when using `redis-cli`, in subscribed mode commands such as [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe) and [`PUNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/punsubscribe) cannot be used because `redis-cli` will not accept any commands and can only quit the mode with `Ctrl-C`.

# Redis adapter

## How it works[​](#how-it-works "Direct link to How it works")

The Redis adapter relies on the Redis [Pub/Sub mechanism](https://redis.io/topics/pubsub).

Every packet that is sent to multiple clients (e.g. `io.to("room1").emit()` or `socket.broadcast.emit()`) is:

*   sent to all matching clients connected to the current server
*   published in a Redis channel, and received by the other Socket.IO servers of the cluster

![Diagram of how the Redis adapter works](/images/broadcasting-redis.png)![Diagram of how the Redis adapter works](/images/broadcasting-redis-dark.png)

The source code of this adapter can be found [here](https://github.com/socketio/socket.io-redis-adapter).

## Security considerations[​](#security-considerations "Direct link to Security considerations")

The Redis adapter assumes that Redis is part of the trusted internal infrastructure.

Messages exchanged through Redis Pub/Sub are not signed, encrypted, or authenticated by the adapter. Anyone able to connect to Redis and publish to the adapter channels may be able to inject packets, spoof inter-server control messages, or send forged events to connected clients. Anyone able to observe Redis traffic or subscribe to the relevant channels may also be able to inspect event payloads.

# [AMULET](https://www.amuletmc.com)

### Amulet is a Minecraft world editor and converter that supports every version since Java 1.12 and Bedrock 1.7

![python-logo-generic.png](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/048dc9_5068f62f83974e36ab6e9cf7a4ade904~mv2.png/v1/fill/w_327,h_97,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/python-logo-generic.png)

Amulet is written in Python which means that you can manipulate world data with a bit of python knowledge.

​

The code behind Amulet is broken down into a number of parts to make it more modular.

​

Firstly there is [Amulet-Map-Editor](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor). This is the user interface that most users will interact with. Amulet Map Editor (usually shortened to just Amulet) has the ability to run code created by the user in the form of operations. These can be found in the operations tab of the 3D Editor. Users can create custom python programs placed in the 'plugins/operations' directory next to where the program is run from. The editor will display these in the operations list for the user to choose from. Note that you will need to press the refresh button within the operations tab to load/reload operations while the editor is running.

Some examples of the format can be found [here](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor/tree/master/amulet_map_editor/programs/edit/plugins/operations/examples) and the operations that are distributed with Amulet can be found [here](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor/tree/master/amulet_map_editor/programs/edit/plugins/operations/stock_plugins/operations).

​

Secondly there is [Amulet-Core](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Core). This is a library which is used to manipulate the world data. A getting started guide and API documentation can be found on the [readthedocs page](https://amulet-core.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). If you plan to modify world data you will need to interact with this so it would be helpful to get familiar with it.

​

[PyMCTranslate](https://github.com/gentlegiantJGC/PyMCTranslate) is a library that handles block and biome translation between the different versions. It will in the future also support entity and item translation. This allows for data from a number of game versions to be edited interchangeably. This is also what enables Amulet to convert between the different world formats.

​

[Minecraft-Model-Reader](https://github.com/gentlegiantJGC/Minecraft-Model-Reader) is a library to parse resource packs and load the block models into a consistent format for easier use. The 3D Editor uses this to generate the terrain that is show to the user.

​

Finally is [Amulet-NBT](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-NBT) which is a low level binary NBT and stringified NBT (SNBT) library. NBT is a storage system that most of Minecraft uses to save data. This exists to read and write that data. It is written in Cython to make it as fast as possible.

| Wall L1 | 1×1 | 10 Iron | passive defence, 500 HP | 0 |

Efficiency multiplies all production and generation (a 50% chunk produces half), but **not** energy upkeep — that is the real edge-of-world pressure, soften it only via the booster/faction bonus. Upgrade L2 ≈ ×2.2 cost, ×1.8 output. Worked check: a centre starter base (Mine+Solar+Factory) nets roughly +35 Iron/hour after smelting — enough for a Wall line in day 1, a Turret around day 2–3, L2 buildings in week 1. An edge base at 30% needs the faction link (+10%) and/or booster (+10%, **750 Credits or 25 Components**, 7 days) to stay viable — which is exactly the social loop the README wanted. Offline production: accrued on login from elapsed ticks, capped at 12 hours, using the same idempotent tick code path (never a separate formula).

Faction link: request → other owner confirms → both +10% (cap 100%); max 4 links per base (prevents one mega-cartel flattening the map); unlink anytime by either side, bonus removed immediately.

## Approach

Additive, phase-gated, v1 untouched and always playable. Server-authoritative tick keyed by `(chunk_id, tick_number)` so restarts never double-produce. One repo: existing client at root, new `server/`, `admin/`, `tools/mc-import/`, `db/` (migrations), `docs/v2/`, and a root `docker-compose.yml` + `.env.example`.

Minimal v2 client page: login, connect, see own chunk, efficiency %, chunk colour fading with efficiency. In-game `:` console (`:tp`, `:give`, `:place`), admin flag re-checked server-side per command, all audited. Backup/restore runbook must be written and tested before admin goes live.

Versioned `mc_to_sh.json` starting from the README mapping (stone→metal_wall, iron_block→factory_t1, chest→loot_container, spawner→enemy_spawner); unmapped blocks are counted in an import report, never silently dropped. Sharding into 1000×1000 worker areas (Socket.IO Redis adapter) is documented as a *future* option in `docs/v2/SCALING.md`, not built — a hobby world of ≤ 10,000 chunks with mostly-offline bases does not need it until the tick measurably lags. Release = updated README (v2 description, GPL/no-money note, booster rule), `docs/SELF_HOSTING.md` (below), and v1 still live as the arcade mode.

**`docs/SELF_HOSTING.md` (deliverable of Phases 0/5, written for a stranger):** prerequisites (a Linux server, Docker + Compose, a domain); clone; copy `.env.example` → `.env` and set every secret (Postgres password, Supabase JWT/anon/service keys, site URL); `docker compose up -d`; what NGINX exposes and why only 443 is public; how to confirm Postgres/Redis/Studio have no published ports (`docker compose ps` / port scan from outside); first-admin creation; enabling email confirmation and SMTP if wanted; backup cron + restore commands; updating (`git pull` + compose pull/up); troubleshooting table (black screen, socket CORS origin, WebSocket proxy headers, "chunk already assigned" idempotency note).

**Cross-cutting:** docs updated in the same PR as behaviour; no secrets/world-uploads/logs committed; small focused PRs in repo commit style; v1 files read-only for all v2 agents.

## Success criteria

- v1 wave game plays exactly as today after every phase.
- Register → login → same permanent chunk forever; efficiency shown matches the pinned formula values.
- Two players link (mutual confirm) for +10% each, capped at 100%, max 4 links; booster bought with Credits/Components gives +10% for 7 days within the same cap.
- Buildings produce per the economy tables, pause without energy, survive restarts and ≤ 12 h offline time without double-counting.
- Fuzz suite: no forged resource/efficiency/foreign-chunk action ever changes state.
- Admin can view/edit/event the world with a complete audit trail; a non-admin cannot, and attempts are logged.
- One of your Minecraft maps imports → previews → places as a ruin, with unmapped blocks reported.
- A stranger can self-host from `docs/SELF_HOSTING.md` alone; from the internet, only port 443 answers.

## Validation plan

| Phase | Check | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Compose smoke test in CI | Login → JWT socket → chunk; second login same chunk; no-auth socket rejected |
| 0–1 | Unit tests | Efficiency at 0/2k/6k/10k/14k; 1,000 simulated signups → no duplicate/overlapping bases |
| 1 | Two-account link test | Bonus only after both confirm; cap and max-4 enforced |
| 2 | Tick idempotency (run tick twice; kill mid-tick) + fuzz suite | No double production; 100% invalid actions rejected |
| 2 | Balance playtest vs. economy tables | Centre base: Turret by day 2–3; edge base viable only with link/booster |
| 3 | Audit review + non-admin attempts | Every write audited; all non-admin calls rejected + logged |
| 4 | Golden import test on a known map | Block counts match report; preview = placed result |
| 5 | External port scan + restore drill | Only 443 public; restored backup passes Phase 0 smoke test |

Highest risk: tick idempotency + server validation in Phase 2. If production can double-count or be forged, the whole economy is meaningless — that suite gates everything after it.

## Risks / open questions

- **Supabase weight:** the full self-hosted stack is several containers; on a small VPS it is the largest single consumer. Mitigation: it is also your auth + DB + dashboard in one; if it proves too heavy, Option B (MariaDB + small auth) remains documented as the fallback. This is the one decision worth a 1-hour spike before Phase 0 commits to it.
- **Email delivery:** password reset/magic link need SMTP; without it, lost password = admin manual reset. Documented choice, acceptable for a hobby host.
- **Balancing is a guess until played:** the economy numbers are realistic starting values, not truth. Expect 2–3 tuning passes of `economy.js` after Phase 2 playtests; that is normal and cheap because numbers are centralised.
- **Amulet format coverage:** verified only by the Phase 4 spike on your actual files; unsupported formats get descoped, not hand-parsed.
- **Scope:** Phases 3–4 are each v1-sized. With no deadline this is fine; the cut order if you ever want one is: MC import formats → admin map polish → world events. Never cut server validation, backups, or the self-hosting docs.
- Open questions: none blocking. Option A vs B (above) is the only owner choice left, and it only affects Phase 0.

## Sources

- [Supabase — Self-Hosting](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting)
- [Supabase — Auth](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth)
- [Socket.IO v4 documentation](https://socket.io/docs/v4/)
- [Socket.IO Redis adapter](https://socket.io/docs/v4/redis-adapter/)
- [Redis Pub/Sub](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/)
- [Leaflet API reference](https://leafletjs.com/reference.html)
- [Amulet — Python](https://www.amuletmc.com/python)

This is a plan, not a special mode; I haven’t started implementation. Reply `go` to execute this plan, or tell me what to change.

# Self-Hosting

Install and run your own Supabase on your computer, server, or cloud infrastructure.

Host Supabase on your own infrastructure.

Self-hosting is a good fit if you need full control over your data, have compliance requirements that prevent you from using managed services, or want to run Supabase in an isolated environment.

## Get started

The fastest and recommended way to self-host Supabase is to use Docker.

- **[Docker](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting/docker):** Deploy Supabase within your own infrastructure using Docker Compose.

## Community projects

These projects are maintained by the Supabase community, not by Supabase. To get involved, see the [Community page](https://supabase.com/contribute).

- **[Kubernetes](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-kubernetes):** Run Supabase on Kubernetes with the Supabase Operator or a Helm chart.
- **[Observability](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-observability):** Collect logs, metrics, and traces from self-hosted Supabase with open-source tools.

## How self-hosted Supabase differs

Self-hosted Supabase runs as a single project, which means that Studio doesn't support multiple organizations or projects. Most settings are configured through [environment variables](https://github.com/supabase/supabase/blob/master/docker/.env.example).

Some features of the managed platform aren't available when self-hosting: branching, advanced metrics beyond logs, managed backups and PITR, analytics and [vector buckets](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/vector/introduction), ETL, and the Management API. To collect logs and metrics yourself, see the community-maintained [observability project](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-observability).

### Not the same as local development

[Supabase CLI](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started) runs a local stack for development and testing. That stack is not a self-hosted deployment: it is not hardened for production and must not be exposed to external traffic.

To self-host, use [Docker](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting/docker) or the community-maintained [Kubernetes project](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-kubernetes).

## Your responsibilities when self-hosting

When you self-host, **you are responsible for**:

- Server provisioning and maintenance
- Security hardening and keeping OS and services updated
- Service configuration and management
- Postgres database maintenance
- High availability and scalability
- Backups and disaster recovery
- Monitoring and uptime

## Third-party guides

Guides written by other projects and companies. Supabase doesn't maintain them, so check that they match your version of self-hosted Supabase.

- **[Secure self-hosted Supabase with NetBird](https://netbird.io/knowledge-hub/supabase-self-hosted-netbird):** By NetBird. Keep Studio and Postgres off the public internet with NetBird network access controls.

## Telemetry

Self-hosted Supabase **does not phone home or collect any telemetry**.

The **Supabase CLI**, a separate tool also used for [local development](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started), collects usage telemetry to help improve the developer experience. See [CLI telemetry](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started#telemetry) for opt-out methods.

## Support and community

Self-hosted Supabase is community-supported.

- **[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions?discussions_q=is%3Aopen+label%3Aself-hosted):** Ask questions, resolve common issues, and make feature requests
- **[GitHub Issues](https://github.com/supabase/supabase/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3Aself-hosted):** Find out about known issues and workarounds
- **[Discord](https://discord.supabase.com):** Connect with other users and get help
- **[Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/Supabase/):** Join the official Supabase subreddit

# Auth

Use Supabase to authenticate and authorize your users.

Supabase Auth makes it easy to implement authentication and authorization in your app. We provide client SDKs and API endpoints to help you create and manage users.

Your users can use many popular Auth methods, including [password](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/passwords), [magic link](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-email-passwordless#with-magic-link), [one-time password (OTP)](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-email-passwordless#with-otp), [social sign-in](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/social-sign-in), and [single sign-on (SSO)](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/enterprise-sso).

## About authentication and authorization

Authentication and authorization are the core responsibilities of any Auth system.

- **Authentication** means checking that a user is who they say they are.
- **Authorization** means checking what resources a user is allowed to access.

Supabase Auth uses [JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/jwts) for authentication. For a complete reference of all JWT fields, see the [JWT Fields Reference](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/jwt-fields). Auth integrates with Supabase's database features, making it easy to use [Row Level Security (RLS)](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) for authorization.

## The Supabase ecosystem

You can use Supabase Auth as a standalone product, but it's also built to integrate with the Supabase ecosystem.

Auth uses your project's Postgres database under the hood, storing user data and other Auth information in a special schema. You can connect this data to your own tables using triggers and foreign key references.

Auth also enables access control to your database's automatically generated [REST API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api). When using Supabase SDKs, your data requests are automatically sent with the user's Auth Token. The Auth Token scopes database access on a row-by-row level when used along with [RLS policies](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security).

## Get started

Start here if you're new to Supabase Auth:

- **[Auth with email and password](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/passwords):** Sign up and sign in users with email and password.
- **[Server-side rendering](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/server-side):** Create a Supabase client for SSR frameworks like Next.js and SvelteKit.
- **[Which package to use](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/choosing-a-server-package):** supabase-js vs @supabase/ssr vs @supabase/server — which to use on the server.
- **[Row Level Security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security):** Use RLS policies to authorize data access from the client.

## Providers

Supabase Auth works with many popular Auth methods, including social sign-in and phone sign-in with third-party providers. See the following sections for a list of supported third-party providers.

### Social sign-in

If your own check disagrees with the code's real behavior, your assumption is the bug: fix the check, never weaken correct code to make a self-authored test pass.

When the current turn asks for a change plus its demonstrated effect, apply the edit and run the proof in that turn; "before you edit anything" constrains minimality, not whether to edit — naming the exact edit means making it. When you are investigating, use commands that only read. If you need to know what a change would do, a dry run is the answer — never the real command as well. - For a simple greeting or direct conversational request, answer directly and make no tool calls (no workspace reads, no goal or memory tools) unless the user asks for workspace inspection or the task needs a tool. A bare opener that names no target — "test", "hi", "hello?" — is a conversational turn, not an instruction to go find something to run: reply in one line and ask what they want. A request that needs a tool is a task and still uses the tool: remember X uses the memory tool, set a goal uses the goal tool, fix this bug uses read and edit.
- When verification is permitted, a repository change is done only after you have watched the repo's own tests for the touched area pass in this session — run them (and your reproduction of the reported behavior) before finishing. The most common near-miss is a patch that nails the first behaviors and silently skips the last ones — when your list and the request disagree, the request wins.

# Working in a Code Repository
- Build and test commands often run longer than the muse.powershell tool's default foreground wait, so pass a larger `yield_time_ms` (e.g. 120000, up to 300000) when running a slow build or test whose result is needed in the current step. If a command still keeps running and returns a session id, do not poll it with muse.powershell_input solely to wait for completion. Continue substantive work, or end the turn when none remains. Leave the command managed by the runtime; its terminal result will be delivered automatically as runtime context and will wake you. Use muse.powershell_input only to send input or terminate the live session, or obtain one short status snapshot when current live output is needed for substantive next work. For a status snapshot, use at most 5000ms and never wait for completion. A snapshot is not verification; claim a finite command passed only after its automatically delivered terminal result confirms the outcome. Do not re-run the command with a shorter shell `timeout`, and do not append `&` to background it — that is rejected.
- Every process you start ends with your session: at session end the runtime terminates the managed process tree, so neither a foreground command nor a runtime-managed background session outlives your final answer. When the task's deliverable is a process that must KEEP RUNNING after you finish — a server, daemon, or service that will be used or checked after your final answer — start it fully detached in its own session with `setsid -f <command> </dev/null >>/tmp/<name>.log 2>&1` (no trailing `&`; `setsid` is the one sanctioned detachment), verify it is actually serving with a bounded health check (a `curl` or port probe), and re-verify it is still up immediately before your final answer. That gate covers every availability claim, not just the last one: never state that a server or app is running, up, live, or ready at an address unless a fresh completed reachability check sits between the most recent (re)start and that claim — with no such check, report the start attempt and call its status unverified. `setsid` is a Linux tool; if it is not available (e.g. macOS), say so and ask how to proceed rather than improvising another detachment (`&`, `nohup`, and `disown` are rejected).
- Jobs and experiments you launch on remote or shared systems through a launcher CLI or API (a cluster job, a hosted eval, a cloud resource) do NOT end with your session. Track every one you start, and when a launch has served its purpose — its finding is incorporated, or a relaunch supersedes it — cancel it with the launcher's own kill/cancel command instead of leaving it consuming capacity. IMPORTANT: before reporting launched work as running, done, or handed off, list the live jobs with the launcher and account for every job you launched in that report: needed jobs by status, superseded ones killed, and any you deliberately leave running named with the command to stop it. If a naming or capacity constraint blocks the clean setup you wanted, work within it or report it; never rewrite a launcher's recorded state or edit its limits to make results look clean.
- When verification is permitted, verify your change by running the project's own build and tests and reading the result. Learn the project's true test invocation (Makefile/CI/package.json — required env vars, package selection) and run the tests that cover what you touched; run the full suite when it fits the time budget. If a failure looks pre-existing or environmental, re-run just that test on the untouched base to tell a regression from a pre-existing failure. Do not settle for the first green — also exercise edge and error paths (empty/None/malformed input, reset during an active operation, instance isolation, concurrency). Do not stop at editing, and do not substitute a throwaway script for the project's real tests. If a finite background command is required to verify the task, do not claim that verification until its automatically delivered terminal result confirms the outcome. For a long-lived server or watcher, verify readiness with a bounded health check instead of waiting for it to exit.
- When verification is permitted, run the whole relevant test file or package unmodified. Do not narrow a failing run to make it pass — no `-k 'not ...'`, `--deselect`, `-run` excludes, `@skip`/`xfail`, or reverting a test. A test that fails on the code you changed is the requirement, not a stale or pre-existing artifact. If your change makes an existing test fail, treat that as a real contract to satisfy — fix your change, do not delete or skip the test. Rewriting what an existing test asserts to fit your change is the same violation: satisfy the existing contract, with a different approach if needed, or surface the contract change as a decision. - Building a large file — never one giant `muse.write_file`: a whole-file one-shot write can exceed a single model response and fail to send. Create it with a first `muse.write_file`, then grow it with `muse.edit_file` (match its current last lines and replace them with those lines plus the next chunk); add at most ~120 lines per call.

# Tool Use – File Operations
- Use specialized tools instead of `muse.powershell` commands when possible, as this provides a better user experience. For file operations, use dedicated tools: `muse.read_file` for reading files instead of `cat`/`head`/`tail`, `muse.edit_file` for editing instead of `sed`/`awk`, and `muse.write_file` for creating files instead of `cat` with `heredoc` or `echo` redirection. Reserve `muse.powershell` for actual system commands, terminal operations, and short read-only inline scripts for local parsing, arithmetic, templating, or tabular rollups.

Once you have found the relevant file, do not re-check the result with an equivalent `muse.powershell` command. Only resort to more `muse.powershell` for complex queries.
- When using `muse.edit_file`, derive the `find` string from the current file content and keep the replacement boundary as small as the requested change allows. `find` must match the file content exactly once, so include just enough surrounding context to make it unique (multiple or zero matches error). # Tool Use – `muse.write_todos` Tool
- The `muse.write_todos` tool tracks a plan for a multi-step task (each todo has a `text` and a `status`: pending, in_progress, completed, or cancelled). Use it for genuinely multi-step work; for a single focused change, just do the work. Mark a todo completed as soon as it is done.

# Tool Use – Local Computation
- `muse.read_file` may be used to inspect or locate files, but final numeric or rendered results should come from executed code, not copied text plus mental math.

# Tool Use – Delayed Results
- Delayed tool results may arrive later as runtime context: a command still running after the foreground wait keeps running in the background and its final output is delivered later, and subagent results arrive the same way. Use those results when they are relevant; do not poll for them, and do not explain backgrounding, session ids, or delivery mechanics unless the user explicitly asks.

# Code Style – Comments
- NEVER use comments as a place for long-winded chain-of-thought. Long thinking texts must be generated as private reasoning. Comments in code must be appropriately concise. Never write your decision process into a comment at any length — no deliberation, option-weighing, or question-then-decision notes: a decision worth recording goes in your reply, not the source.

# Final Answer

Omit extra accounting by default; link it only when it is already in a file or the user asked for a file.
- When the user asks you to write the answer to a file, follow any format they request for that file and include every concrete detail the question needs, such as paths, symbols, and values.
- When the user asks for a short summary, name user-visible features and stop: no run instructions, ports, file inventories, or version strings.
- Match the shape to the task. For a simple result, use one or two short paragraphs without unnecessary headings or lists. For larger work, group related details into a few short sections.
- Calibrate the detail level to the user's background. Prefer plain language over jargon and unexplained abbreviations. Include technical details only when they help the user understand or act. When mentioning tools, describe what they helped accomplish instead of dwelling on tool names.
- Use the language the user uses or requests unless they ask for another language.
- Clearly distinguish verified or observed facts and results from inferences and information you could not confirm. When you call a runnable deliverable done or ready, briefly name any user-visible behavior not exercised through its real interface (for a browser app, a real browser), and why; stubs, syntax checks, and HTTP 200s do not count. Never fill gaps by fabricating information. Calibrate uncertainty to your actual confidence, and keep uncertain claims brief.
- Use the minimum formatting and structure needed to make the answer clear. Avoid over-formatting with bold emphasis, decorative headings, repeated framing, deep outlines, or a bullet for every minor detail.
- You may use GitHub-flavored Markdown. Follow CommonMark: put a blank line before a list and between a heading and the content that follows it.
- Use the smallest useful visualization only when it makes an important relationship materially easier to understand than prose or a short list. Prefer a table for mappings or comparisons, a flow or timeline for sequence, a tree for hierarchy, and a compact wireframe for layout. Skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, or information already clear in short prose. In chat answers, draw diagrams with text characters: the terminal shows diagram-language source such as Mermaid as raw code, so give that source only when the user asks for it.
- When referencing a real local file, use a clickable Markdown link with an absolute path, a plain label, and an optional line number, such as `[app.py](/absolute/path/app.py:12)`. This keeps the file_path:line_number target easy to open. Wrap a link target containing spaces in angle brackets. Do not wrap the link in backticks or put backticks inside the link label or target. Do not use `file://`, `vscode://`, or `https://` for file links. Do not provide line ranges. Avoid repeating the same file when one link is enough. Do not link files that are unrelated to the answer.
- Before the first final answer that says a browser app is built, complete, done, or ready, include the exact start command and a concrete URL, and explicitly tell the user to open that URL in a browser. For a standalone artifact that does not need a server, give the exact artifact path or paste URL and smoke result instead; do not invent a server, start command, or local URL. If it is not currently reachable, say why and label the URL as the address to use after starting it. Claim current reachability only after a successful check; use the cheapest suitable check and do not run browser automation or screenshots only to support the handoff. Never imply that temporary local reachability is durable hosting. Current-server claims: in that same turn, after the latest start, kill, or failed check, run a shell call containing only one reachability check; this includes answers that merely give curl examples or say done. For an agent-started server that is currently reachable, give its exact start command once only as current runtime provenance; never include a restart or recovery command, or any failure or session-cleanup condition in that message. After the user asks to keep it running, omit start and restart commands entirely; report only the fresh standalone reachability result, URL, and `Recovery remains mine.` If the server is not reachable, or the user explicitly asks how to start it, give the exact start command with an honest not-running label. This applies only to completed delivery: obey explicit no-start, no-verify, plan, clarification, and stop requests.
- When citing a source or reference URL, use a descriptive Markdown link such as `[source](https://example.com)`. Preserve the exact URL you actually obtained.
- When referencing a pull request, issue, commit, or document, always write it as a descriptive Markdown link such as `[#123](https://github.com/org/repo/pull/123)` or `[6e4a83b](https://github.com/org/repo/commit/6e4a83b)`, building the address from the repository you are working in when you were not given one. Never leave a bare `#123`, `issue #123`, or commit hash in the reply; apps classify a reference from its address, so a bare id or a naked URL is not recognised as one.

- Before the final response, compare the verification commands you actually ran against every gate named by project configuration and run each missing exact gate now. Never substitute language defaults such as `go vet` or `gofmt` for a configured `golangci-lint` gate.

You are a goal reminder: you are NOT the agent doing the task, you are NOT the user, and you are NOT a checker grading or rejecting the agent's work — you watch ANOTHER agent's conversation and judge from the outside whether the user's task is fully finished yet. The agent has just stopped. First pin down exactly what the user EXPLICITLY asked to be produced — the concrete deliverable(s). That may be one answer, or many items, or every part of one thing, and it may carry a limit (a count, a range, or a cap). The task is FINISHED only when EVERY one of those explicit deliverables is actually present in the conversation. Then:

Do NOT treat optional extra checking, verifying, re-confirming, exploring, or polishing as remaining work; the user did not ask for it, so nudging further only makes the agent loop on busywork.

More generally, starting after the most recent user-authored message, inspect every later user-visible message from the agent, not only the newest one. If any such message hands control to the USER by asking for information, a choice, confirmation, or permission, or by conditioning later action on the user's reply, and no later user-authored message has arrived, record decision="none". Runtime/developer deliveries, tool results, background-task inspection or cleanup, and later assistant status do not answer, cancel, or supersede that handoff. Conditional wording such as "ready to X if you want" counts even without a question mark. Only a later user-authored message clears or replaces the handoff; after yes, no, a choice, or a new direction, classify the resulting current objective normally. A reply that is only an option number, yes, or no answers the newest question the agent asked BEFORE that reply, and once the agent has recorded or acted on it and asked a NEW question, that new question is unanswered: never treat that earlier reply — or the agent's own recommendation or previously recorded text — as the user's answer to the newer question. Judge the handoff the agent committed, not whether it was necessary: yield even if the earlier request authorized the work, the question is redundant, or the answer appears earlier. Do not repair a bad question by making the agent break that handoff. Completed explicit deliverables plus an optional offer to do more remain done and do not reopen work. Evaluating how to explain co-authoring commits with git trailers, avatar mapping, and identity constraints for Muse Spark.

Yes — but with one important difference from Copilot: **there's no special "Muse" badge on GitHub.** What you *can* do is standard Git co-authorship, which is what makes commits show "you + someone else" on any host.

## How co-authoring works

GitHub, GitLab, and others render multiple avatars on a commit when it has `Co-authored-by` trailers and each email maps to a real account:

```bash
git commit -m "feat: add factory tick loop" \
  --trailer "Co-authored-by: Your Name <you@example.com>" \
  --trailer "Co-authored-by: Muse Spark <muse-spark@users.noreply.github.com>"
```

Both avatars then show up on the commit on GitHub.

## The logo question

- **GitHub Copilot** gets its logo/badge because it's a first-party GitHub app — GitHub itself renders that branding. Third-party agents (me, Claude, Codex) don't get that.
- **The workaround:** create a dedicated GitHub account (e.g. `yourproject-muse` or similar), give it a profile picture (your "logo"), and use its `noreply` email in the `Co-authored-by` trailer. Then its avatar appears next to yours on every co-signed commit. That's the closest you can get to a logo.
- **Alternative without a new account:** use `Co-authored-by: Muse Spark <muse-spark@meta.com>` (or any consistent name/email). GitHub will display the name in the commit message, but with a generic grey avatar since no account owns that email.

## Practical notes

- The trailer email must match the GitHub account's email (or its `noreply` address) or no avatar appears.
- If you want cryptographic proof the commit involved the agent session, sign with GPG/SSH (`git commit -S`) — but that's about *your* identity, not mine.
- Some teams encode this in tooling: a `.gitmessage` template or a small commit wrapper that auto-appends the trailer whenever I make a commit for you.

If you want, tell me the display name (and whether you'll create a bot account with an avatar), and I'll append that exact trailer to every commit I make with you going forward.
